title: 2D & 3D Signs
description: Flat 2D cutouts and dimensional 3D letterforms combined to give storefronts depth and presence, whether mounted on a wall or built into a larger sign package. This hybrid format is one of the most requested storefront upgrades because it works for almost any brand: a flat backer panel carries a logo mark or secondary graphic while raised 3D letters catch light and cast shadows, so the sign reads clearly by day and glows or highlights well by night if lit. Because 2D and 3D elements are fabricated as separate layers, businesses can mix materials  a painted aluminum backer with acrylic 3D letters, for example  to hit a specific look and budget without redesigning the whole sign.
features: Custom shapes cut to any logo outline

faqs.q: What's the difference between 2D and 3D signs?
faqs.a: 2D signs are flat cutouts while 3D signs have depth and dimension, often lit from within.

faqs.q: Can these be used both indoors and outdoors?
faqs.a: Yes, we build both interior and exterior-rated versions depending on material choice.

faqs.q: How thick are the 3D letter returns?
faqs.a: Return depth typically ranges from 3in to 5in, chosen based on letter size and viewing distance.

faqs.q: Can you combine 2D backer panels with 3D letters?
faqs.a: Yes, layering a flat 2D panel behind 3D letters is a popular way to add contrast and depth.

faqs.q: How do I know if I need 2D, 3D, or a combination?
faqs.a: It usually comes down to viewing distance and budget  flat 2D graphics are more economical for close-up interior use, while 3D letters add shadow and presence for street-facing storefronts; combining both is common when a business wants a layered, dimensional logo look.

title: Back Lit Reverse Channel Letters
description: Reverse-mounted channel letters that push a soft halo glow outward against the wall behind them, giving a premium, upscale look popular for boutique and hospitality branding. Because the light source faces the wall rather than the street, halo-lit letters create an ambient glow around each letterform instead of a bright, direct light  a look many boutique retailers, hotels, and upscale restaurants choose specifically because it reads as understated and high-end rather than loud. The effect depends heavily on wall material and color, so halo letters are typically specified alongside a site visit to confirm the wall will produce the intended glow.

seoTitle: Back Lit Reverse Channel Letters (Halo Lit) | Custom Signage

faqs.q: Why choose halo lit over front lit letters?
faqs.a: Halo lit letters give a softer, premium ambient glow rather than a bright, direct light source.

faqs.q: Do halo lit letters need a standoff mount?
faqs.a: Yes, they're mounted on standoffs to allow the light to project onto the wall behind them.

faqs.q: How far from the wall are halo letters mounted?
faqs.a: Standoffs are usually set between 1in and 2in from the wall to control the width of the halo glow.

faqs.q: Do halo letters work well on dark-colored walls?
faqs.a: Yes, the glow effect actually shows up strongly on darker brick, stucco, or painted walls.

faqs.q: Does wall color affect how the halo looks?
faqs.a: Yes  lighter or textured walls tend to diffuse the glow more broadly, while smooth dark walls produce a tighter, more defined halo ring around each letter.

title: Blade Signs
description: Double-sided projecting signs mounted perpendicular to a building so pedestrians and passing traffic can read them from either direction  a staple for walkable retail strips. Because a blade sign hangs out from the facade rather than lying flat against it, it catches the eye of foot traffic approaching from either side of the sidewalk, which is why they're so common outside medical offices, downtown storefronts, and strip mall units where a flush wall sign alone isn't enough. Local sign codes usually govern how far a blade sign can project and how high it must sit above the sidewalk, so this format almost always involves a permit as part of the install.
